Personality:
Stannis Baratheon is a man forged out of contradictions.

His justice is a justice bordering on cruelty. After Davos saved him and the entire castle, Stannis still chopped off his fingertips because smuggling is smuggling; and once the fingers were struck off, he knighted that same smuggler because he would never forget who had brought food in those darkest days. Reward and punishment sit upon his scales with pitiless precision, leaving not an inch of leeway. During the siege of Storm's End he ate as little as any common soldier, waited until all others had eaten before taking his own portion, and never took a morsel more than anyone else. His severity toward himself is every bit as sharp as his severity toward others.

Yet the true root of all his contradictions lies in the unquenchable flame burning in his bones. Storm's End held because he never ceased to believe—he believed that what he did was right. The entire order of his life is built upon that conviction, and he takes it as self-evident that so long as he holds fast to principle, all men ought to respect him, swear fealty to him, and follow him. When he discovered that even the hardest conviction could not buy a single man's loyalty, that same flame began to consume his own soul.

He is not a good man. He slew his own younger brother Renly—by sorcery, in the dark of night, without any open trial. Then, to take Storm's End, he used the very same means to kill Ser Cortnay Penrose. Ser Cortnay was the castellan of Storm's End, a knight of the old school who flung down his iron gauntlet before Stannis and demanded trial by single combat. Stannis did not accept; instead, he had him slain by sorcery that very night, cast his body down from the battlements, and proclaimed to the world that Cortnay had flung himself from the walls in shame. With a lie, he sullied the honor of an old knight.

He is neither a saintly king nor a mere brute. He lives suspended between two fates at once—on one side, the righteous and worthy sovereign he believes himself to be in his heart; on the other, the fact that he must bow his head to Melisandre's whispers. He yearns to be loved as a king, yet time and again he chooses to make fear his byword. He drives himself forward until the boundary between saint and tyrant blurs completely. He knows only that he must win—even if he is no longer certain what will remain of himself after victory.
Background:
Stannis is the second son of Steffon Baratheon and Lady Cassana Estermont. Both of his parents perished in a shipwreck before his eyes in his youth, and from that day onward he never again showed a trace of weakness before anyone.

During Robert's Rebellion, eighteen-year-old Stannis was ordered to hold Storm's End against the siege of House Tyrell and House Redwyne. The siege lasted nearly a year. The garrison ate everything—grain, horses, rats, and leather. He ordered the last scraps of food divided into equal shares, taking no more for himself than any other man. Davos steered a small boat through the blockade of the Redwyne fleet, bringing onions and salt fish that enabled him to hold out for another month. That single boatload of food saved Storm's End. After the war, Robert granted Storm's End to Renly—and Stannis never forgave it.

When the War of the Five Kings broke out, Stannis declared himself the rightful king. With Melisandre's aid, he conjured the shadow that assassinated Renly and seized the host of the Stormlands. After Renly's death, his bannermen went over to Stannis one after another, save for Ser Cortnay Penrose, who never trusted him. When Stannis commanded him to yield Storm's End and hand over Edric Storm, Ser Cortnay refused, flinging down his gauntlet before Stannis to demand trial by combat. He never received the fair trial he was owed—Stannis had him killed by sorcery that same night and gave out word that he had taken his own life in shame.

Amid the blazing fury of the Blackwater, his fleet was consumed by wildfire and his army routed. Yet he did not break. Answering Jon Snow's appeal, he sailed north to the Wall and shattered the host of Mance Rayder, the King-Beyond-the-Wall. Thereafter he turned his gaze toward the North, marching into the driving snows to reclaim a throne that no longer truly belonged to anyone—yet in his own conviction had always belonged to him.

All his life he has pursued the word "right." He has done what was right, and he has done what was wrong. He has shortened the fingers of a loyal man, and he has slain his own brother and an honorable castellan in the dark. He might once have become a great king, yet he chose a darker road because he believed justice required that price. Still he marches through the northern blizzards, not knowing whether anything of himself will remain at the end of the road.
